 Edited  by  Arturo Conde, CEPF® Updated on October 20, 2026, 9:55am ET | Fact Checked Add SmartAsset as a preferred source on Google Share President Donald Trump announced on Sept. 9 that every adult U.S. citizen would receive a $5,000 payment if Republicans keep control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. 1 That could mean $10,000 for a married couple. At the moment, there is no approved check, rebate or tax credit to claim . The proposal remains a campaign pledge, and its implementation would likely require congressional action and funding. Here’s how the dividend might work, who may qualify and what your family stands to get.
 While the proposed dividend remains uncertain, a financial advisor may be able to help you review your tax planning strategy and evaluate opportunities to manage your finances under existing tax laws.

 Find Your Advisor Trump’s $5,000 Promise and What Needs to Happen First
 Trump made the announcement at the Republican National Committee’s first midterm convention in Dallas, calling the payment the “Trump Dividend.” 2 He compared it to a company paying out profits, saying it would be “very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.”
 Four days later, the president doubled down on his midterm dividend promise while speaking at the Amgen Irish Open. He said the country could “easily” afford the payments and added, “I always keep my pledge.” 3 
 Neither appearance changed the basic hurdle: winning both chambers can’t put money in anyone’s account without a law to authorize and fund the payments.
 Other presidents and candidates have tied cash to election results. On Jan. 4, 2021, the day before Georgia’s Senate runoffs, President-elect Joe Biden told voters in Atlanta that if they elected Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, “those two-thousand dollar checks are going out the door,” referring to COVID-19 stimulus payments. 4 
 After Democrats won both seats, House Ways and Means Chairman Richard Neal said the American Rescue Plan ’s $1,400 pandemic checks, following December’s $600 payments, “finishes the job on the President’s promise to provide $2,000.” 5 
Campaign promises like these are generally legal. In Brown v. Hartlage (1982), the Supreme Court ruled that the First Amendment protects a candidate’s pledge to give voters a benefit when it would need normal government approval. 6 
The Election Law Blog called Trump’s pledge “almost certainly protected by the First Amendment against bribery or vote buying charges,” citing Brown v. Hartlage as the leading case. 7 
 The Trump dividend would require congressional action to authorize and fund the payments.
 Who Could Qualify for the Trump Dividend
 At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, the president promised to “issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” Assuming he is referring to every citizen old enough to vote, that would be roughly 250 million people, based on 2026 Pew Research Center data. 8 
 The amount pledged to be paid out could be about $1.25 trillion (250 million × $5,000). For a comparison, that would be more than three times larger than the third round of stimulus checks passed in 2021, when the IRS issued over 175 million payments totaling more than $400 billion. 9 
 Vice President JD Vance said wealthy Americans could be excluded, which would lower the total cost. 10 The administration hasn’t shared details on that potential exclusion, so the actual cost can’t be estimated yet. Here’s what different households could receive based on the pledge as described:
 How Much a Household Could Receive From the Trump Dividend
 Household Possible Payment Based on the Pledge What Is Still Unclear 
 Single adult citizen $5,000 Possible income limit 
 Married couple, both citizens $10,000 Whether higher earners would be excluded 
 Married couple with two children $10,000 based on the two adults Whether children could qualify 
 One citizen and one noncitizen spouse Potentially $5,000 Treatment of mixed-status households 
 A financial advisor can help you plan to use a salary bonus, tax refund or other windfall, whether you decide to pay down debt, build emergency savings or invest for future goals. 
 Despite the administration’s proposal, Americans largely remain skeptical. An Economist/YouGov poll found that only one fifth of registered voters (21%) believe Trump will “definitely or probably” follow through on the pledge if Republicans keep control of Congress, while 57% said they don’t believe he will follow through on the campaign promise. 11

 The Constitution establishes that no money can be drawn from the Treasury without an appropriation made by law. 12 That means Congress would have to authorize and fund the program before any payments could go out.
 The Tax Foundation estimates that paying $5,000 to 250 million adults eligible to vote would cost about $1.25 trillion. 13 The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) separately estimates that a $5,000 dividend would cost more than $1.2 trillion if paid in 2027. 14 
 While Vice President JD Vance has said tariff revenue could help reduce the cost, the nonprofit projects that new tariffs would raise roughly $1.4 trillion in net revenue from 2026 through 2035. 15 
 If this estimate holds, one round of Trump dividend payments would use almost 90% ($1.25 trillion ÷ $1.4 trillion) of that 10-year projection. However, the Tax Foundation said that the federal government is already expected to run a deficit of nearly $1.9 trillion in fiscal year 2027. 
 The CRFB calculates that adding a one-time dividend would push that deficit up to $3.1 trillion.
 How Trump Dividends Compare With Past Payments and Promises
 Comparing past federal programs and proposed dividends could show which ones were approved, how they were funded and who received the money. Every direct payment in the table below that reached households had congressional funding behind it. The proposals that did not get funding were never paid.
 Timeline of Past Payments and Proposals
 Year Payment or Proposal Amount Congress Funded It? Paid? 
 2008 Economic stimulus payment 16 Up to $600 individual, $1,200 jointly, plus $300 per qualifying child Yes Yes 
 March 2020 CARES Act payment Up to $1,200 per adult Yes Yes 
 Dec. 2020 Second COVID payment Up to $600 per adult Yes Yes 
 2021 American Rescue Plan payment Up to $1,400 per eligible person Yes Yes 
 2025 DOGE dividend proposal 17 About $5,000 per taxpaying household proposed No No 
 2025 Tariff dividend proposal 18 At least $2,000 per person proposed, excluding high earners No No 
 2025 Warrior Dividend 19 $1,776 for qualifying service members Yes, through existing military housing funds Yes 
 A campaign pledge does not authorize a payment. For the Trump dividend, legislation passing both chambers and becoming law would matter more than the election result.
 The proposed $5,000 per adult would exceed all three pandemic-era checks combined. An adult who received the full amount in each round got $3,200 ($1,200 + $600 + $1,400).
 Taxes could also affect how much you keep. The 2021 stimulus checks weren’t taxable, and the Warrior Dividend was tax-free because it was paid as a military housing allowance. Congress has not created the Trump dividend, so its amount, eligibility rules and tax status have not yet been confirmed.
 Two More Midterm Election Payments You May Get
 The Trump administration announced two additional payments alongside its proposed $5,000 dividend. It will send $500 Affordable Care Act refunds to almost one million people in 30 states and is offering a one-time $90 Medicare Part B premium rebate.
 The $500 refunds go to people in states who buy insurance through HealthCare.gov and receive no financial assistance toward their monthly premiums . The White House said the money comes from excess fees collected to run the exchange. 20 
 Federal health officials at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services say 20.8 million people are eligible for the $90 rebate. 21 Eligibility is limited to people living in the U.S. with Part B coverage under Original Medicare.
 The rebate excludes people whose Part B costs are already paid by Medicaid , higher earners who owe IRMAA and anyone enrolled in a private Medicare Advantage plan. The agency is sending the money in October, either straight to a bank account or by mailed check, as a credit toward that month’s Part B bill.
 Bottom Line
 Keep the proposed dividend out of your household budget until Congress approves funding and sets the eligibility rules and payment method. One qualifying adult might receive $5,000 and two might get $10,000, but neither amount is guaranteed. Continue covering bills and meeting savings goals with income you already have. Any payment that eventually arrives can then go toward overdue expenses, high-interest debt, emergency reserves or longer-term priorities.
 Tips for Managing Your Money
 A financial advisor can help you build a budget that works without a government check and plan where the money could go if one arrives. Finding a financial advisor doesn’t have to be hard. SmartAsset’s free tool matches you with vetted financial advisors who serve your area, and you can have a free introductory call with your advisor matches to decide which one you feel is right for you. If you’re ready to find an advisor who can help you achieve your financial goals, get started now .
 Money you don’t need for bills or debt could go into a high-yield savings account for emergencies or near-term expenses. For longer-term goals, you might consider investing through a brokerage account . Compare fees and minimum balances before choosing either option.
